title: B-Tree Indexes & Composite Index Ordering
description: Master B-tree structure, left-prefix rule for composite indexes, equality vs range column positioning.

data.text: The **B-tree (Balanced Tree)** index is the workhorse of PostgreSQL. It maintains sorted key order from root to leaf pages. For **composite indexes** (indexes across multiple columns), the order in which columns are declared dictates which queries can utilize the index.
The Left-Prefix Rule for Composite Indexes

If you create an index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at)`: queries filtering by `tenant_id` can use the index; queries filtering by `tenant_id` AND `status` can use the index; but queries filtering ONLY by `status` or `created_at` CANNOT use the index efficiently because they skip the leading column.

data.title: Golden Rule: Equality Columns First, Range Columns Last
data.content: Ordering columns in composite indexes for maximum seek efficiency.

data.text: Why Ordering Matters: Equality Then Range

Within a composite B-tree, place equality columns first and the range or sort column last. An index on `(tenant_id, created_at)` can seek directly to one tenant and then scan a contiguous block of dates, so `ORDER BY created_at` needs no sort. Swap the order and the planner has to scan many separate ranges.

data.title: Equality, then range, then sorted output
data.content: Because the index is ordered by created_at within each tenant, the range scan returns rows in the requested order and the plan shows no Sort node.
data.code:
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_tenant_created
ON orders (tenant_id, created_at DESC);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT id, created_at
FROM orders
WHERE tenant_id = 7
  AND created_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_tenant_created on orders
--   Index Cond: ((tenant_id = 7) AND (created_at >= ...))
--   Buffers: shared hit=6

data.title: Functions and casts break the index
data.text: Wrapping the indexed column in a function or cast makes the predicate non-sargable: `WHERE created_at::date = '2024-05-01'` cannot use an index on `created_at`. Write it as a range (`created_at >= '2024-05-01' AND created_at < '2024-05-02'`) or create an expression index on the exact expression the query uses.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Composite indexes must be searched from the leftmost column outward.
Always place equality (`=`) filter columns first in composite index definitions.
Place inequality / range (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`) filter columns at the end.
